q: Who may submit a change request on a project, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: Only the project manager, after review
Any stakeholder, from inside or outside
Only members of the change control board
Only the sponsor, in writing
explanation: Any stakeholder may request a change, and change requests may be initiated internally or externally to the project.

q: Testing finds a weld that does not meet its specification. Which type of change request is needed to fix it?
options: Preventive action
Corrective action
Update
Defect repair
explanation: A defect repair is an intentional activity to modify a nonconforming product or product component.

q: Productivity has been behind plan for three weeks. The team proposes extra pair work to bring performance back in line with the plan. Which type of change is this?
options: Corrective action
Defect repair
Update
Configuration audit
explanation: A corrective action realigns the performance of the project work with the project management plan. A preventive action would keep future performance aligned before it slips.

q: Before the baselines are approved, the team keeps refining the scope. How are these changes handled in a predictive project?
options: Each one needs a formal CCB decision
They must be rejected until execution
They are not formally controlled yet
They go straight into the change log as approved
explanation: In predictive approaches, changes are not formally controlled until baselines are established. Once a baseline exists, all changes go through the formal process.

q: A customer phones the project manager asking for a change to a baselined deliverable. What should happen first?
options: Make the change, since the customer asked
Document it in writing as a change request
Refuse, since it was not written down
Ask the team to estimate it informally and start
explanation: Changes can be initiated verbally, but they should be documented in writing and entered into the change or configuration management system.

q: What should a change request typically include before it can be approved?
options: Only the requester's name and the date
The final design of the changed product
The sponsor's signature in advance
Estimated schedule and cost impacts
explanation: Change requests should typically include information on the estimated schedule and cost impacts before they can be approved.

q: A change request must wait two weeks for the next CCB meeting. What should the project manager do in the meantime?
options: Continue the planned work and analyze the impact
Stop all of the project's work until the board decides
Start the change to save time
Withdraw the request to avoid delay
explanation: While awaiting the CCB's decision, project managers continue to execute planned tasks while analyzing the impact and risks of accepting or rejecting the change.

q: Which document establishes the change control board and documents the extent of its authority?
options: The team charter
The communications management plan
The change management plan
The requirements traceability matrix
explanation: The change management plan establishes the CCB (also known as a steering committee), documents its authority, roles and responsibilities, and describes how the change control system will work.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Change management plan

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Change management plan

q: Which plan specifies which project artifacts are under configuration control, so that changing them needs a formal request?
options: The quality management plan and checklist
The configuration management plan
The resource management plan
The benefits management plan
explanation: The configuration management plan specifies which artifacts are subject to configuration control; changes to these require a formal change request.

q: The CCB has approved a change to the product. What may still be needed before the work starts?
options: A completely new project charter for the change
A vote of the whole project team
A new competitive bid for the work
Sponsor approval, if not on the board
explanation: Depending on the change, customer or sponsor approval may be required after CCB approval, unless the customer or sponsor is a CCB member.

q: In an adaptive project, a stakeholder proposes a new feature. What happens to the proposal?
options: It is added to the backlog and prioritized
It needs a formal CCB approval first
It is rejected until the next release
The team builds it in the current iteration at once
explanation: A proposed change is recorded as a product backlog item; an impact analysis evaluates its effect and sets its priority. There is usually no formal approval process.

q: The product owner gives a proposed change a low priority. What does that mean in an adaptive project?
options: The change is formally rejected
The change must go to the CCB
The change is effectively deferred
The team must build it next iteration
explanation: A lower priority essentially means the change is deferred. Not adding it to the backlog, or removing it, means it is rejected.

q: Where is the current status of every submitted change recorded?
options: The issue log
The change log
The risk register
The lessons learned register
explanation: The change log is a comprehensive list of changes submitted during the project, with their current status; the disposition of every change request is recorded there.

q: The CCB rejects a change requested by a regional manager. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the decision quiet to avoid conflict
Implement part of the change anyway
Ask the CCB to vote again next week
Record it and tell the regional manager why
explanation: Deferred or rejected change requests are communicated to the person or group who requested them, and the disposition is recorded in the change log.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Approved change requests

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Approved change requests

q: Which process implements approved change requests?
options: Manage Project Execution
Close Project or Phase
Identify Stakeholders
Develop Schedule
explanation: Approved change requests are implemented via the Manage Project Execution process, which also implements corrective and preventive actions and defect repairs.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Approved change requests

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Approved change requests

q: An approved change adds a new deliverable. What may it also require?
options: Nothing, as approval is the last step
Removing it from the change log
New estimates, schedule and risk assessments
A brand-new project manager just for the change
explanation: Approved change requests may require new or updated cost estimates, schedule adjustments, resource requirements and risk assessments, and updates to the plan and documents.

q: Two months after a change was implemented, what should the project manager check?
options: That the old change log has been deleted
That the change gave the desired result
That the requester has paid for it
That no one remembers the old plan
explanation: Changes are made to improve the original plan; their results should be monitored to ensure they yield the desired results.

q: After an approved scope change, which records should be updated?
options: Only the team's task board on the wall
Only the final report at closure
Nothing until the project closes
The plan, baselines and affected documents
explanation: Outputs of Assess and Implement Changes include project management plan updates (any component, including baselines) and project document updates such as the change log.

q: Why is the schedule model updated with every approved change?
options: So it shows all of the current known scope
So the original baseline is deleted
So the critical path never changes
So variances no longer appear in reports
explanation: The schedule model is updated with approved changes so it represents 100% of the current known scope and the current project management plan.

q: Without anyone deciding, small additions keep entering the scope while time and budget stay the same. What is this?
options: Fast tracking
Rolling wave planning
Scope creep
Resource leveling
explanation: Scope creep is the uncontrolled expansion of product or project scope without adjustments to time, cost and resources. A change control system combats it.

q: A proposed change has a large cost but would bring a large benefit. Which technique helps decide whether it is worth it?
options: A burndown chart
Cost-benefit analysis
Planning poker
A RACI chart for the team
explanation: Assess and Implement Changes uses data analysis such as alternatives analysis and cost-benefit analysis, and decision-making techniques, to decide on changes.

q: The sponsor, who chairs the CCB, tells the team to add a feature directly and skip the board. What should the project manager do?
options: Add it straight away, since the sponsor decides
Refuse and escalate to the PMO
Ask the team to vote on it
Raise a change request so its impact is analyzed
explanation: Once a baseline exists, all changes go through the formal process, with impact analysis and a documented decision. This protects the baseline and gives the sponsor the information to decide.

q: What should the project manager do about the rooftop bar?
options: Let the foreman continue, since a director asked for it
Stop the ordering, raise a change request and analyze it
Refuse the bar, since the scope is baselined
Build it and adjust the baseline afterwards
explanation: The renovation is baselined, so the new scope needs a written change request, an impact analysis and a decision by the CCB or designated person before any work or ordering continues.

q: How should the front desk's request for a group-booking feature be handled?
options: As a backlog item prioritized by the product owner
As a formal change request to the renovation's CCB
Built at once by the team, as it is small
Rejected until the renovation ends
explanation: The booking app is built with an adaptive approach: the request becomes a product backlog item, and impact analysis and the product owner's priority decide when, or whether, it is built.

q: The CCB approves the rooftop bar. What should happen next?
options: Start building at once, before updating anything
Close the change log entry without a note
Update the baselines and plan, then implement
Ask the director to manage the bar alone
explanation: Approved changes may need new estimates, schedule adjustments and risk assessments; the plan, baselines and change log are updated, and the change is implemented through Manage Project Execution.

q: Which THREE are possible decisions on a change request in a predictive project?
options: Approved
Rejected
Deferred
Ignored
Self-approved by the requester
Hidden from stakeholders
explanation: Each documented change request is approved, deferred or rejected by a designated person or the CCB; more information may also be requested.

q: Which TWO are outputs of the Assess and Implement Changes process?
options: Approved change requests
Change log updates
Team charter
Product roadmap
Bid documents
explanation: Figure 2-10 lists approved change requests, project management plan updates (any component) and project document updates (change log).

q: Which TWO pairs of areas does impact analysis of a change examine, according to the example flow for project changes?
options: Schedule and finance
Risk and stakeholders
The team's holiday plans
The vendor's profit margin
The office seating layout
explanation: Figure 2-11 shows impact analysis across scope, finance, schedule, resources, stakeholders and risk before the decision.

q: Match each type of change request with an example.
right: Extra pair work to get back on plan
Training before a risky task starts
Fixing a weld that failed its test
Adding a new idea to the design document
explanation: Corrective actions realign performance with the plan; preventive actions keep future performance aligned; defect repairs modify nonconforming products; updates reflect modified or added content.

q: Complete each statement about change control.

blanks.text: The group that reviews, approves, defers or rejects changes is the
In adaptive projects, changes are managed mainly through
Uncontrolled scope growth without more time or money is

explanation: The CCB decides on changes in predictive projects; backlog management replaces formal change requests in adaptive ones; scope creep is what change control prevents.
